readerTitle: The big order that pays less than it costs
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (식자재 유통업체 + 호텔 그룹의 대량 주문) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 대량 특가 주문은 평균 원가가 아니라 그 주문이 '새로 더하는' 비용으로 판단하고, 그 계산은 남는 처리 능력 안에서만 성립한다.
misconception: 평균 원가보다 낮은 가격의 주문은 무조건 손해이고, 반대로 변동비만 넘으면 얼마든지 받아도 된다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (고정비·변동비, 한계비용, 특별주문 의사결정)

factChecks.note: 단골 가격: $26 − $14 = 상자당 $12. $18로 맞춰 주면 상자당 $4로 줄어듭니다.

cards.title: The big order that pays less than it costs
body: You run a small food distributor. Your van delivers oil, flour, rice and canned goods to 60 local restaurants.
A hotel group calls with the biggest order you've ever had. The catch: they want **$18 a case**. Your accountant says each case costs you $21.

image.label: Delivery van loaded with stacked food cases outside a hotel
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 배송 밴 옆에 식자재 상자가 높이 쌓여 있고, 뒤로 호텔 건물. 상자 하나에 "$18" 가격표, 장부에 "Cost $21" 메모. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Yes or no?
body: The order: 2,400 cases over 12 weeks at $18. Regulars pay $26.
Your $21 has two parts: $14 that comes with each case (goods, packing, fuel) and $7 of rent, staff and van lease spread across every case. You pay that $7 either way.

options.feedback: You avoid a loss that isn't real. Rent and staff get paid either way, so each case at $18 still leaves $4 you'd never see otherwise.

options.text: Interested, but first check it fits our current capacity
options.feedback: Each case leaves $18 − $14 = $4. That holds only if you can deliver without adding costs. So you check.

options.text: Counter at $21 so we break even
options.feedback: Sounds safe, but your real floor is $14, not $21. Push too hard and the hotel walks, taking $4 a case with it.

cards.title: What one hotel case leaves you
body: The $7 of rent and staff isn't on this list. Saying yes doesn't add it. Saying no doesn't remove it. If nothing else changes: 2,400 × $4 = **$9,600**.

breakdown.label: Left over
breakdown.detail: Extra money toward rent and profit

cards.title: Say you chose B. Now the warehouse.
body: You ship 800 cases a week and can handle 900 with your van and crew. The hotel needs 200 a week.
The first 100 fit. The other 100 need overtime and a rented van, adding about $6 a case.

options.text: Take all 200 a week and absorb the overtime
options.feedback: The 1,200 cases that fit earn $4,800. The 1,200 beyond capacity cost $20 each and lose $2,400. Lots of extra work for $2,400.

options.text: Offer 100 a week at $18 and the rest at $22
options.feedback: The fitting cases earn $4,800. If the hotel takes the extra at $22, that's another $2,400. If not, you keep $4,800 with no overtime.

options.text: Take all 200 and push some regular deliveries back a day
options.feedback: No overtime, but you trade your $26 customers' reliability for $18 cases. Lose one regular and the deal can turn negative.

cards.title: Why the same case suddenly cost more
body: Up to 900 cases a week, one more case costs $14. Past that, it costs $20, because overtime and a rented van come with it.
That's **marginal cost**: the cost of one more unit. It isn't constant. It jumps when you run out of room. So "is the price above cost?" needs a follow-up: above *which* cost, at *this* volume?

image.label: Step chart: cost per extra case jumps from $14 to $20 at 900 cases
image.brief: 계단형 그래프. 가로축 "Cases per week", 세로축 "Cost of one more case". 900 지점까지 $14로 평평하다가 $20으로 한 계단 올라감. 계단 위치에 작은 렌트 밴과 시계(야근) 아이콘.

cards.softwareNote: Serving one more user costs almost nothing until you hit a step: a bigger server plan or another support hire. Before a big-account discount, check whether the deal fits current capacity or forces the next step.

cards.title: Say you chose B. A regular calls.
body: The hotel signs. Word gets around. Rosa, who runs a busy trattoria and has paid $26 a case for six years, asks for the hotel price.

options.feedback: She's happy, but her cases drop from $12 left over to $4. Regular prices are what pay your rent and staff.

options.text: Explain the hotel's terms: huge volume, quiet-day delivery, 12 weeks only
options.feedback: The low price is tied to conditions that keep costs down. Rosa sees it isn't favoritism, and your base price holds.

options.text: Give her a small loyalty discount to keep the peace
options.feedback: Fair for a valued customer, but you pay to fix what an explanation might solve for free. Others may ask next.

cards.title: Say you chose B. The hotel wants a year.
body: The hotel offers a full-year contract: 400 cases a week at $18.
That needs a second van, a driver and more space: about $2,400 a week in new fixed costs.

options.text: Sign. It grows the business by half
options.feedback: Each case now carries $14 plus $6 of new costs: $20. At $18 you lose $800 a week, and your costs are built around one customer.

options.text: Counter at $22 with a minimum-volume commitment
options.feedback: Each case leaves $2 after the new costs, about $800 a week. The minimum protects you if orders shrink after you hire.

options.text: Decline and keep only the short deal
options.feedback: No new risk, but you may walk away from a profitable account. A counteroffer costs nothing to try.

cards.title: The $4 logic only works on spare room.
body: Pricing near the cost of one more unit suits spare capacity and one-off deals. On average, your prices must also cover rent and staff, or the business slowly drains.
Once you hire or lease for a customer, those costs stop being "paid anyway." They belong to that deal. And if that customer leaves, they stay with you.

cards.title: Judge an order by what it adds, not by your average cost.
body: A low-price bulk order is worth it when it covers the costs it adds, fits your spare capacity and stays fenced off from your regular price.
list: **Decision 1 · Fixed vs variable costs:** the $7 of rent and staff gets paid either way.
**Decision 2 · Marginal cost:** one more case cost $14, until capacity ran out.
**Decision 3 · Fixed vs variable costs:** full-price customers carry the fixed costs, so the deal price can't spread.
**Decision 4 · Operating leverage:** new fixed costs for one customer raise your risk if they leave.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down how much more you could sell this month without overtime, hiring or new equipment. That's your room for special deals.
